doc.title: Milt Fillius interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 18, 2000

title: The class of 1944 and the war years
summary: Why his class was unusual: no Latin or Greek requirement, the war, and graduating in 1947.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: I have a quote here from you, from a number of years ago, and you said that the class of 1944 was a rare breed, one of the best Hamilton has ever had.
What was the reason for that?

I don’t know. We had a librarian named Pilkington who wrote a book when he left about the college, and it was said that the class of 1944 was terrible and never should have been admitted. And I think his reason was maybe the same reason — that was the first class that did not require a basic background of study of Latin or Greek. It was the first time that we could get in with a romance language. I got in for example with French or German, one of the two. And Latin and Greek had been the requirement ever since. And if you base your education on that it’s a little different than — more stilted I think than other forms of education. I think the war had a lot to do with it because everybody I know who went to that war and came back in one piece is a better man for it. And we had some guys who might otherwise not have been as successful. I don’t think I would have been if I’d just gone through college and had not gone to law school and gone to California and all the rest of it. I certainly wouldn’t have been. And the result is that that class has turned out some pretty good people that have been very good to this college.
Those years were called the “crazy mixed up years?”
I want to make sure I get that right, where a lot of the fellas came back and graduated a couple of years later than they might have.

We all did. But a lot of us didn’t. A lot of my class never did graduate. They went elsewhere, but they still come back to our reunions and they consider this their home. I don’t know what the percentages are but there are a lot of them. And many people went to graduate school and I could have done that. When I came back from the war I was 12 hours short of a degree. I elected to come back in the summer and pick up those 12 hours before I went to law school in the fall. But I could have not done that, I could have just
gone to law school. But with the twelve hours I was able to graduate, which I did in ’47 instead of ’44.
